title: Outdoor Site Selection, Sun, Drainage and Water Access

content.overview: Outdoor cultivation begins with the site. Sun exposure, soil depth, drainage, slope, irrigation access, prevailing wind, surrounding vegetation and equipment access determine which management problems will appear later and how difficult they will be to correct.

vocabulary.definition: The compass direction a slope faces, which influences sun exposure and drying.
Movement of excess water away from the active root zone.
The depth of soil or media that roots can effectively explore.
Local environmental conditions that differ from the broader weather pattern.

sections.title: Sun and season set the energy budget
sections.body: A site should receive adequate light during the intended production season without avoidable shading from trees, buildings or terrain. Seasonal sun angle and day length change, so a site that looks open in spring may behave differently later.

sections.title: Drainage and soil depth affect roots
sections.body: Low areas, compacted zones or shallow soils can create persistent saturation or limited rooting volume. Soil testing and field observation should precede large plantings because irrigation cannot correct every physical site limitation.

sections.title: Water availability must be practical
sections.body: Irrigation source, delivery capacity and seasonal availability should be evaluated before planting. Outdoor demand changes with weather, crop size and planting density, so water planning should include both supply and distribution.

sections.title: Access and surrounding land matter
sections.body: Equipment width, field traffic, neighboring crops, wind exposure and nearby vegetation can affect operations, pest movement and pollination risk. Site planning should include the landscape around the crop rather than only the planting bed.

workedExamples: A low field corner that remains wet days after rain should be treated as a drainage risk before planting rather than corrected later with more fertilizer.
A site with excellent sun but unreliable midsummer water access may require a different crop plan or irrigation strategy.
commonMistakes: Choosing a site from sun exposure alone.
Assuming all parts of a field have the same drainage.
content.practicalApplication: Walk the site after rain and during sunny conditions, map shade, slope, wet zones, access routes and water points, review soil information, and document constraints before deciding plant spacing or irrigation design.
content.summary: Site selection is preventive cultivation management. Light, soil, drainage, water, access and surrounding land use should be evaluated before plants make those constraints expensive to fix.
